title: Full Cutoff
passage:
Brackwell keeps an unusually complete record of its own light. Every pole in the town has been photographed and logged, its fixture type checked against the code the council adopted in 2016, and the tally is read out each March. Ninety-four percent of the street lighting is now full cutoff. The installed output is down about a fifth since the code passed, and a survey plane that flew the valley in 2017 and again last year measured less light leaving it the second time. The figure goes into the county report. It also went onto the sign at the town line, which since 2022 has carried the words DARK SKY COMMUNITY under the elevation.

Forty minutes up the ridge road, Nuria Feltrin keeps a record of her own, and it is harder to put on a sign. A photometer bolted to the dome at Vellin Ridge has read the brightness of the empty sky between the stars on every clear night since 2003. Across the ten seasons since the code passed, the zenith reading improved by about three percent. Feltrin will not credit that to Brackwell. The photometer was recalibrated in 2018, and the two autumns after 2019 were dry enough to leave the valley with less dust in it than the twenty-year average; either of those, she says, would move a three percent figure on its own. What she is prepared to state is the other series, the one the observatory actually schedules against. In 2015, the last season before the code, the faint-galaxy program reached its target depth on sixty-one nights. Last season it managed thirty-eight.

The lamps that stood in Brackwell before the code were low-pressure sodium, and they were, by any ordinary measure, worse. They were unshielded, they were orange, and residents complained about them for thirty years. But nearly everything they emitted sat inside a band about two nanometers wide, and a piece of glass in front of the detector took that band out of the sky at a cost of well under one percent of the range the observatory works in. What replaced them is white, shielded, and in total no brighter. It is also spread from one end of the visible spectrum to the other. There is no filter for white. Fewer photons now arrive at the dome than in the sodium years, and a smaller share of the sky can be kept clear of them, which is how a slightly better zenith number and twenty-three lost nights ended up describing the same ten seasons.

Malcolm Rieger, who wrote the model the county's audit is scored against, thinks the argument has been allowed to run too far. Uplight from unshielded fixtures, he says, is the dominant term in any sky-glow budget by a wide margin; fix that and what is left are corrections on corrections. "A county buys street lighting," he says. "It is not obliged to buy telescope time." Feltrin grants him the half she thinks is his, and grants it without hedging: at Ashcombe, thirty kilometers down the valley, no code was ever adopted, uplight rose through the same decade, and every number the ridge keeps got worse together. Where the fixtures are unshielded the fixtures are the story. But Brackwell's code governs street lighting, and the worst single source now visible from the dome is not on a pole. Two hectares of greenhouse at the north edge of town are lit through the winter nights by fixtures that point down at the plants and stand indoors, and the code was never written to reach them. Feltrin can pick the greenhouse out by color: on clear December nights the north horizon brightens and the ratio of red to blue in what the photometer reports shifts in a way nothing else in the valley does. The operation is in full compliance. It was never asked for any.

Feltrin's request is modest and has gone nowhere. She would like two more lines printed beside the compliance percentage each March: the share of the sky the observatory can still work in, and the name of the largest source in the valley that no code covers. Neither is anyone's duty to produce. She does not expect the sign at the town line to come down, and she says she would not ask for it, because Brackwell did what it was asked to do in the units it was given. The units were poles. The ridge counts photons, and for ten seasons the two records were not describing the same valley.
— Owen Frisk

full cutoff = a fixture built so that no light leaves it above the horizontal
zenith = the point of the sky directly overhead

questions.prompt: What are we told about Brackwell's street lighting since 2016?

options.text: The code reached every light in the valley, so nothing installed there now throws any light upward.
The council reports progress, but its audit has never established what share of the poles the code reached.
Nearly all of it is shielded now, and the town's total installed output has come down.
Shielding was left to owners to adopt, and enough of them declined that the valley's uplight rose.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 1. WHY-KEY (C): 'Ninety-four percent of the street lighting is now full cutoff. The installed output is down about a fifth since the code passed.' C recasts ninety-four percent as 'nearly all of it', full cutoff as 'shielded', and the fifth as output that 'has come down' — paraphrase, not lift. This is one of the unit's flat, confident keys (law 10): nothing about it is hedged, and the option written to sound careful (B) is the wrong one. WHY-NOT-A (trap: quantifier_upgrade plus scope error): the sign at the town line says DARK SKY COMMUNITY and the audit sounds exhaustive, so 'every light in the valley' feels like the natural reading of a near-total figure. It fails twice — the figure is ninety-four percent, not all, and it covers street lighting only, while the greenhouse at the north edge of town stands outside the code entirely. WHY-NOT-B (trap: over-hedged contradiction): built as the measured-sounding wrong answer so that reaching for the cautious option scores nothing here. The passage says the opposite: 'Every pole in the town has been photographed and logged', and the share is stated to the percent. WHY-NOT-D (trap: wrong_location): every element of it is true somewhere in the piece — it is Ashcombe's story, thirty kilometers down the valley, where 'no code was ever adopted, uplight rose through the same decade'. A reader who remembers a town in the passage whose lighting got worse attaches it to the wrong town.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the sodium lamps Brackwell used before the code?

options.text: They were replaced because the council wanted fixtures that would draw less power for the same light.
Nearly all their light fell inside one narrow band, which the observatory could screen out at little cost.
They put less total light over the valley than the shielded fixtures that took their place.
The glass that blocked them cost the observatory most of the blue end of the range it works in.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (B): 'nearly everything they emitted sat inside a band about two nanometers wide, and a piece of glass in front of the detector took that band out of the sky at a cost of well under one percent of the range the observatory works in.' B states the same two facts in different words — concentration in one band, and removal at a small price. Confident and specific, not hedged. WHY-NOT-A (trap: outside_knowledge): the efficiency of modern lighting is the standard real-world reason for exactly this kind of replacement, and the passage does give the lamps a motive for being unpopular — 'residents complained about them for thirty years' — so a passage-blind solver has no way to rule it out. The text never mentions power, cost, or the council's reason for the switch. WHY-NOT-C (trap: direction reversal on a real quantity): the passage does compare the two eras by total light, which makes the comparison feel checked, but it runs the other way: what replaced the sodium is 'in total no brighter', the installed output is down about a fifth, and 'Fewer photons now arrive at the dome than in the sodium years'. WHY-NOT-D (trap: surface_word_match): it recycles the passage's own filter-and-range vocabulary and sounds like the trade-off such a filter would involve. The stated cost is 'well under one percent of the range', and the band removed was sodium's, which the passage describes as orange, not blue.

questions.prompt: The zenith reading over the ridge improved by about three percent across the ten seasons. What does the text suggest about that improvement?

options.text: That the 2018 recalibration accounts for it, the instrument having read differently after that date.
That the code did improve the sky over the ridge, though by less than the shielding work would suggest.
That monitoring of this kind cannot establish whether a lighting code has worked anywhere.
That it is too small to be told apart from other things that moved over the same years.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 2. The passage supplies two candidate explanations and a sentence about their size — 'The photometer was recalibrated in 2018, and the two autumns after 2019 were dry enough to leave the valley with less dust in it than the twenty-year average; either of those, she says, would move a three percent figure on its own' — and reports that 'Feltrin will not credit that to Brackwell', without saying why in so many words. The stem restates the figure without indicating what the text makes of it. WHY-KEY (D): if either of two unrelated changes would by itself move a number of that size, the number cannot be assigned to any one cause; that is the inch the reader walks. WHY-NOT-A (trap: too_literal, with an added commitment): it takes one of the passage's two candidates and promotes it to the explanation. The text says either would move the figure, not that the recalibration did; picking one is exactly the move Feltrin declines. WHY-NOT-B (trap: quantifier softened into a confident attribution): the most natural reading for a solver who assumes a code that shielded ninety-four percent of a town's poles must have bought something, and it even sounds modest. The passage withholds the credit outright, and 'less than the shielding work would suggest' invents a comparison the text never makes. WHY-NOT-C (trap: too_far): a two-step leap from one ambiguous series to a claim about the method in general. The same monitoring is what establishes the Ashcombe result, where 'every number the ridge keeps got worse together' under no code at all.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Rieger's case that shielding is what counts?

options.text: The writer allows his point where fixtures are unshielded, but not his verdict on what is left over.
The writer shares his view that a county's lighting is not there to serve one observatory's instruments.
The writer treats his budget model as an evasion that the ridge's own record has now discredited.
The writer finds him broadly borne out at Brackwell, with the unregulated greenhouse a minor exception.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / attitude), anchored in paragraph 4. WHY-KEY (A): the concession is made in the text's own voice and made flatly — Feltrin 'grants him the half she thinks is his, and grants it without hedging', and the passage adds its own verdict sentence, 'Where the fixtures are unshielded the fixtures are the story.' What is refused is the remainder of his claim, that once uplight is fixed 'what is left are corrections on corrections': the paragraph then produces the worst single source visible from the dome and shows that it is not a shielding problem at all. WHY-NOT-B (trap: role_or_attribution_swap — the TYPE-005 signature): 'It is not obliged to buy telescope time' is the most quotable line in the passage and it is Rieger's, given in his own voice. A solver reading for tone rather than for the speaker hands it to the writer, who in fact spends the rest of the paragraph bounding it. WHY-NOT-C (trap: polarity overshoot): dismissal overshoots a text that concedes Rieger a real point without hedging and calls his term dominant where it applies; nothing in the piece calls his model an evasion, and Ashcombe is evidence for him, not against him. WHY-NOT-D (trap: measured-sounding weight reversal): written to feel as qualified as the key, so that reaching for the moderate option decides nothing. It reverses the paragraph's weighting — the greenhouse is 'the worst single source now visible from the dome', which is the opposite of a minor exception, and it is the passage's reason for not letting Rieger's account stand at Brackwell.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: That the ridge's losses followed a decade in which the valley's population and its lighting both grew.
That a greenhouse kept lit all winter is the one thing now standing between the ridge and a usable sky.
That the valley's lighting is judged by a count of fixtures, which is not what reaches the dome.
That the observatory has lost nights because the total light over the valley kept rising through the decade.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text gist), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (C): the gap between what is counted and what arrives is the spine of the piece and closes it. Paragraph 1 is entirely an inventory of poles and fixture types; paragraph 2 sets the observatory's own series against it; paragraph 3 explains why a shielded, dimmer town can still cost the ridge twenty-three nights; the verdict names the mismatch directly — 'The units were poles. The ridge counts photons, and for ten seasons the two records were not describing the same valley.' C states that without reusing a run of the passage's wording. WHY-NOT-A (trap: outside_knowledge): growth is the ordinary explanation for a darkening problem anywhere, and the passage does report a worsening over a decade, so nothing on the page marks the claim as foreign until you look for it. Brackwell's installed output fell over that decade and the text never mentions population at all. WHY-NOT-B (trap: scope_error / detail-as-main, distorted): the greenhouse is the passage's most concrete villain and a solver who fixes on paragraph 4 will reach for it. It is a sub-point inside the coverage argument, and 'the one thing now standing between' overstates a text whose ridge also lost nights to a change in the color of compliant street lighting. WHY-NOT-D (trap: surface_word_match on the passage's counting language): 'lost nights', 'total light' and 'the valley' are all the text's own terms, and the drop from sixty-one nights to thirty-eight is real, so the causal story assembles itself. The passage rules the cause out: the installed output is down about a fifth, the survey plane 'measured less light leaving it the second time', and fewer photons now reach the dome than before.

generator_meta.topic: dark-sky policy around an observatory — why a town can pass its lighting audit while the sky over the telescope becomes less usable
